blocks.c: Reading is a daytime word for an activity mostly practiced at night. The lamp goes off, the phone stays on, and one more chapter becomes a unit of time. An app built for readers has to take the dark hours seriously, and this one does — in two places, which this chapter visits in order.

The first is the Aa sheet you met last chapter. Beneath the type controls sits a row of painted squares, each one a theme for the page itself. Dark and dim, for low light. True black, which on an OLED screen switches the pixels off entirely — the page becomes the dark, and the battery quietly thanks you. Light, cream, sepia and tan, for daylight and for readers who like a page that remembers paper. Nord and forest, cooler and greener, for eyes that find the warm tones cloying. Tap through them now; the page re-dresses itself around your place without losing it.

And at the end of the row, custom. Choose any two colors — one for the page, one for the ink — and the reader derives everything else: the dimmed labels, the borders, the quiet in-between shades. Two decisions, one theme, entirely yours. If you have ever wanted a page the exact color of your reading lamp, this is where that happens.

The page, though, is only half the room. Close a book and the shelf is still there — the home screen, the menus, the series pages — and by default they all wear dark. If black might not be your cup of tea, change the whole room, not just the page: the app-wide themes live in Settings, and they are the same palettes, plus the same two-color custom, applied to everything outside the book. A cream shelf around a sepia page. Black everything. A forest-green app holding a tan paperback. The combinations are your business.

The two are deliberately separate. The reader has its own themes, inside the book, so the page you tuned at midnight is not undone by the shelf you brightened at noon. Set each one once, and both will keep.
Darkness is not a feature. It is a courtesy — to your eyes, to the person asleep beside you, and to the battery, in that order.

One honest limit. The comic reader stays dark under every theme, deliberately: pictures carry their own light, and a bright margin around a night scene helps nobody. That is a decision, not an omission, and prose is unaffected by it.
You are, at this point, reading a book you have reshaped twice. It remembers all of it, and it will remember it tomorrow. On to filling the shelf.
